cards.title: Stale Instruction Files Override the Code in Coding Agents: A One-Sentence Fix
cards.what: A paper tested 40 Python projects where the instruction file asks for one convention and the code uses another. Without a fix, 90.1% of agent choices followed the stale file. One sentence in the user-level instruction file giving existing code precedence raised code-following from 4.2% to 91.4% and test pass rate from 89.4% to 100%.
cards.why_you: You rely on CLAUDE.md in every repo, including the workflow kit installed across your projects, so stale instructions are a real risk. A one-sentence user-level change is cheap, and the paper measured it on Claude Code.

cards.title: What the Specification Did Not Say: Specification-Oracle Gaps in Test-Graded Coding-Agent Benchmarks
cards.what: A paper defines a specification-oracle gap: benchmark tests that need names, paths or messages the task description never states. On SWE-Milestone, 25 of 98 milestones had such a test, and affected build units failed in 80.6% of runs versus 48.4%. The ranking held up, but scores shifted. The authors release an audit tool.
cards.why_you: You rely on review gates and evals of agent workflows. This shows how a test-graded benchmark can reward guessing upstream names, which is useful when judging benchmark claims. No project needs action now.

top.headline: Coding-agent benchmarks can demand details the task never states
top.summary: The paper notes that coding-agent benchmarks describe a task in natural language but grade it with tests taken from the upstream project. Passing those tests can require information the description never states, such as a constant's name, a module path or an exact message. The authors call this a specification-oracle gap.
